answers: The ipv6 dhcp relay command should be applied to interface Gig0/0.
questions.explanation:
A DHCPv6 relay forwards client requests toward a server when the server is on another link; it is not itself the address server.

1) Start with the question: First identify where each piece of IPv6 configuration comes from. Router Advertisements communicate on-link prefixes, default-router information and flags. SLAAC lets a host construct its own address; a DHCPv6 server is not required to hold a lease for that SLAAC address.
2) Work through it: Interpret flags independently: A permits autonomous address formation from a prefix, O indicates other information such as DNS through DHCPv6, and M indicates managed address configuration. Stateless DHCPv6 supplies extra information; stateful DHCPv6 allocates managed addresses.
3) Apply the distinction: For stateful DHCPv6, follow Solicit → Advertise → Request → Reply. For stateless information, an Information-request can obtain extra parameters. The default router is learned from Router Advertisements, generally using the router’s link-local address, rather than being an ordinary DHCPv6 gateway option.

EUI-64 derives an interface identifier from a MAC with defined bit changes; privacy mechanisms can use other identifiers. questions.question: Under which circumstance would a router usually be configured as a DHCPv4 client?
options: The router has a fixed IP address.
The router is meant to provide IP addresses to the hosts.
The administrator needs the router to act as a relay agent.
questions.explanation:
A home or edge router can be a DHCP client on its WAN interface and receive its address from the ISP.

1) Start with the question: Decide whether the device is a client, server or relay. A new IPv4 client initially lacks a usable address and may not know a DHCP server. The server leases an address with configuration such as the mask, gateway and DNS servers.
2) Work through it: Follow DORA: Discover locates servers, Offer proposes a lease, Request identifies the chosen offer, and Acknowledgment confirms it. Initial discovery and selection use broadcast behavior; a renewal toward a known server can use unicast.
3) Apply the distinction: Check the layer named in the question. The IPv4 limited broadcast is 255.255.255.255; the Ethernet broadcast is FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. DHCP uses UDP server port 67 and client port 68. A relay forwards client requests between subnets because routers do not normally forward local broadcasts.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not confuse an offer with final confirmation, or renewal with rebinding/expiration. A 169.254.x.x self-assigned address usually indicates that no usable DHCP lease was obtained. On Cisco IOS, show ip dhcp binding displays server leases; ip address dhcp makes an interface a client.

1) Start with the question: Identify the layer and the information a device uses. Ethernet switching operates on MAC addresses within a LAN; IP routing forwards packets between networks using a routing table. A device can combine several functions without making those functions identical.

questions.question: A network administrator is analyzing the features that are supported by different first-hop router redundancy protocols. Which statement describes a feature that is associated with HSRP?
options: HSRP uses active and standby routers.
It allows load balancing between a group of redundant routers.
It uses ICMP messages in order to assign the default gateway to hosts.
answers: HSRP uses active and standby routers.
questions.explanation:
HSRP has an active router that forwards for the virtual gateway and a standby router ready to take over.

1) Start with the question: Start with the host’s view: it needs a stable default gateway even when one router fails. A first-hop redundancy group supplies a virtual gateway, backed by multiple physical routers. The host uses the virtual IP and the associated virtual MAC.
2) Work through it: For HSRP, identify the active router that forwards and the elected standby that is ready to replace it. Higher priority is preferred; preemption allows an eligible higher-priority router to reclaim the active role. Default hello/hold timers are three and ten seconds unless configured otherwise.
3) Apply the distinction: Trace failure in order: the active device fails, the standby misses hellos, the standby becomes active, then forwarding continues using the virtual identity. The host should not need a different gateway address because a physical router changed.
❌ Common mix-ups: Keep protocol families distinct: HSRP is Cisco proprietary, VRRP is standards-based, and GLBP combines redundancy with gateway load sharing. Priority influences election, while the operational state shows what a router is doing now. A higher priority alone does not prove it is currently active.

questions.question: The address pool of a DHCP server is configured with 10.7.30.0/24. The network administrator reserves 5 IP addresses for printers. How many IP addresses are left in the pool to be assigned to other hosts?
questions.explanation:
A /24 has 254 usable host addresses before subtracting any excluded addresses in the prompt.

1) Start with the question: Start with the prefix or subnet mask, not the host’s last octet. Each 255 mask octet contributes eight network bits; partial octets contribute the number of leading binary ones. For example, 252 is 11111100, which contributes six network bits.
2) Work through it: Compute the address count from host bits: 2^(32 − prefix) total IPv4 addresses. In an ordinary multi-access subnet, subtract the network and broadcast addresses to get usable hosts. Then subtract explicitly excluded/reserved addresses that actually fall inside that subnet, counting each only once.
3) Apply the distinction: Treat exclusion ranges as inclusive: last − first + 1. A /24 normally has 254 usable addresses, /25 has 126, /26 has 62, and /27 has 30. An excluded gateway address is a reservation, not an additional network/broadcast deduction.
❌ Common mix-ups: A reservation and an active lease are not the same thing. Check whether the requested answer is total addresses, usable hosts or remaining leases. For /31 and /32, ordinary network/broadcast subtraction is not applied in the same way; use the context stated in the question.

questions.question: Which of the following statement is true?
options: A switch creates separate collision domains but one broadcast domain. A router provides a separate broadcast domain.
A switch creates a single collision domain and a single broadcast domain. A router creates a single collision domain.
A switch creates a single collision domain and separate broadcast domains. A router provides a separate broadcast domain as well.
A switch creates separate collision domains and separate broadcast domains. A router provides separate collision domains.

questions.explanation:
A switch separates collision domains by port; a router separates broadcast domains by interface.

1) Start with the question: Identify the layer and the information a device uses. Ethernet switching operates on MAC addresses within a LAN; IP routing forwards packets between networks using a routing table. A device can combine several functions without making those functions identical.

It looks up the destination MAC to forward a known unicast; it floods an unknown unicast within the VLAN, excluding the arrival port. A router chooses a route using the destination IP and the best matching routing entry.
3) Apply the distinction: Distinguish local delivery from off-subnet delivery. An endpoint uses its mask to identify remote destinations and sends those frames to a gateway’s MAC address. Its packet still carries the remote destination IP; the gateway does not become the final IP destination.
❌ Common mix-ups: A collision domain, broadcast domain and IP subnet are related design concepts, not synonyms. Full duplex permits simultaneous sending/receiving. Throughput is successfully transferred data per time; it differs from the theoretical capacity of a link.

questions.question: The address pool of a DHCP server is configured with 10.19.44.0/24. The network administrator reserves 3 IP addresses for servers. How many IP addresses are left in the pool to be assigned to other hosts?

Then subtract explicitly excluded/reserved addresses that actually fall inside that subnet, counting each only once.
3) Apply the distinction: Treat exclusion ranges as inclusive: last − first + 1. A /24 normally has 254 usable addresses, /25 has 126, /26 has 62, and /27 has 30. An excluded gateway address is a reservation, not an additional network/broadcast deduction.
❌ Common mix-ups: A reservation and an active lease are not the same thing. Check whether the requested answer is total addresses, usable hosts or remaining leases. For /31 and /32, ordinary network/broadcast subtraction is not applied in the same way; use the context stated in the question.

questions.question: How is given the IP Address 172.16.199.25 and the subnet mask 255.255.252.0. What is the CIDR notation for this address?

1) Count the FULL octets first. The mask 255.255.252.0 starts with 255 and 255. Each 255 is a full octet = 8 ones (1111 1111). So 8 + 8 = 16. That is where the 16 comes from. (The 4th octet is 0, so it adds 0 ones.)
2) The only tricky octet is the 3rd one: 252. Add the bit values from the left: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 252, so it is 1111 1100 → six 1s.
3) Add everything: 8 + 8 + 6 + 0 = 22 → /22. (Same thing written short: 16 + 6 = 22.)

Octet by octet: 255 → 8 · 255 → 8 · 252 → 6 · 0 → 0 = 22 ones.

❌ Why the other prefixes are wrong: /23 = 255.255.254.0 (seven 1s in the 3rd octet) · /21 = 255.255.248.0 (five 1s) · /20 = 255.255.240.0 (four 1s).

💡 Memory table for the "odd" octet: 128 = 1 bit · 192 = 2 · 224 = 3 · 240 = 4 · 248 = 5 · 252 = 6 · 254 = 7 · 255 = 8.
💡 The prefix depends ONLY on the mask. The IP address itself does not change the answer (so the .100 vs .199 typo in the options doesn't matter).

questions.question: What is the most compressed valid format of the IPv6 address 2001 :0db8:0000:0016:0000:001b: 2000:0056?

✅ Start with: 2001:0db8:0000:0016:0000:001b:2000:0056. Two rules compress it:
Rule 1 – In each group, drop LEADING zeros only: 0db8 → db8 · 0000 → 0 · 0016 → 16 · 001b → 1b · 0056 → 56.
Rule 2 – A run of all-zero groups may be replaced by "::", but only ONCE in the whole address.
Result: 2001:db8:0:16::1b:2000:56 (the :: replaced the second all-zero group, the first zero group stays as a single 0).

❌ The options that contain TWO "::" are invalid (you could not tell how many zero groups each one hides) → this kills the first two options.
❌ The options that turn 2000 into 2 are wrong: 2000 has trailing zeros, which must NEVER be dropped. 2000 and 2 are different numbers. (That also kills the third option.)

💡 Remember: leading zeros can go, trailing zeros stay; "::" only once.

questions.explanation:
✅ Link-local IPv6 addresses start with FE80::/10 (in practice you see fe80::…). They are created automatically on every IPv6 interface and only work on the same local link (they are never routed). So FE80::261:2EFE:FE10:765 is link-local.

❌ FDF8:F535:82EF::53 → starts with FD = Unique Local Address (FC00::/7), the IPv6 "private" range.
❌ 2001:0db8:85a3:… → starts with 2 = global unicast (2000::/3). (2001:db8 is the range reserved for documentation examples.)
❌ 2401:db00:… → also starts with 2 = global unicast (public internet address).

💡 Quick table: FE80 = link-local · FC/FD = unique local (private-like) · 2 or 3 = global (internet) · FF = multicast · ::1 = loopback.

1) Start with the question: Interpret the IPv6 notation before considering configuration methods. An IPv6 address has eight 16-bit groups written in hexadecimal, and special ranges identify roles such as loopback or link-local communication.
2) Work through it: Leading zeros in a group can be omitted. One consecutive run of all-zero groups can be replaced with ::, but :: may appear only once in an address so expansion is unambiguous. The loopback address ::1 refers to the local host itself.
3) Apply the distinction: Link-local addresses come from FE80::/10 and operate on a local link. IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement to resolve link-layer information; IPv4 uses ARP instead.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not change nonzero digits while compressing an address, or mistake link-local for global reachability. A scope identifier may be needed when a device has multiple interfaces with link-local destinations.

questions.question: At which OSI layer is the data stream broken up into segments that include source and destination port numbers?
questions.explanation:
✅ Layer 4 (Transport) takes the data stream from the upper layers and cuts it into SEGMENTS. Each segment gets a header with the source port and destination port numbers (that is how the receiver knows which application the data belongs to, e.g., 443 for HTTPS).

❌ Network (L3) → makes PACKETS with IP addresses, not ports.
❌ Session (L5) → opens, manages and closes conversations between applications.
❌ Data Link (L2) → makes FRAMES with MAC addresses.

💡 PDU ladder: Data (L5-7) → Segment (L4) → Packet (L3) → Frame (L2) → Bits (L1). Keyword match: "ports" = Transport, "IP" = Network, "MAC" = Data Link.

1) Start with the question: Identify the layer and the information a device uses. Ethernet switching operates on MAC addresses within a LAN; IP routing forwards packets between networks using a routing table. A device can combine several functions without making those functions identical.
2) Work through it: A switch learns the source MAC and ingress port of an arriving frame. It looks up the destination MAC to forward a known unicast; it floods an unknown unicast within the VLAN, excluding the arrival port. A router chooses a route using the destination IP and the best matching routing entry.
3) Apply the distinction: Distinguish local delivery from off-subnet delivery. An endpoint uses its mask to identify remote destinations and sends those frames to a gateway’s MAC address. Its packet still carries the remote destination IP; the gateway does not become the final IP destination.
❌ Common mix-ups: A collision domain, broadcast domain and IP subnet are related design concepts, not synonyms. Full duplex permits simultaneous sending/receiving. Throughput is successfully transferred data per time; it differs from the theoretical capacity of a link.

questions.question: Which information is included in the header of UDP segment?
questions.explanation:
✅ A UDP header is very small (only 8 bytes) and has just 4 fields: source PORT number, destination PORT number, length, and checksum. So "port numbers" is the answer.

❌ IP addresses → live in the IP header (Layer 3), not in the UDP segment.
❌ MAC addresses → live in the Ethernet frame header (Layer 2).
❌ Sequence numbers → belong to TCP (they are used to put data in order and resend lost data). UDP does none of that; it is "connectionless": just send and hope.

💡 Why does UDP exist? Because it is fast and light. It is used for DNS queries, DHCP, VoIP calls, video streaming and online games, where speed matters more than perfect delivery.

questions.question: During the data encapsulation process which OSI layer adds a header that contains MAC addressing information and a trailer used for error checking.
questions.explanation:
✅ Layer 2 (Data Link) is where data becomes a FRAME. It adds a HEADER with the source and destination MAC addresses, and a TRAILER called the FCS (Frame Check Sequence). The receiver recalculates the FCS: if it doesn't match, the frame is corrupted and is thrown away.

❌ Network (L3) → adds IP addresses (no trailer).
❌ Transport (L4) → adds port numbers (and sequence numbers for TCP).
❌ Session (L5) → manages conversations; doesn't add MAC info.

💡 Only Layer 2 has BOTH a header and a trailer. Keywords "MAC" + "trailer" + "error checking" = Data Link.
💡 Remember: MAC addresses change at every hop (every router rewrites the frame), while the IP addresses stay the same end-to-end.

questions.question: Which protocol allows you to securely upload files to another computer on the internet?
questions.explanation:
✅ SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) sends files through an encrypted SSH connection on port 22. Nobody on the path can read your files or password. That is "secure upload".

❌ HTTP → used to load web pages, and it is not encrypted (HTTPS is the secure version).
❌ NTP → Network Time Protocol: keeps clocks in sync. It doesn't transfer files.
❌ ICMP → used by ping and for error messages. It doesn't transfer files.

💡 Don't confuse: FTP (20/21, not encrypted) · TFTP (69/UDP, tiny, no security) · SFTP (22, encrypted). If the word "secure" appears with file transfer, choose SFTP.

questions.question: Move each of the protocol on the left to its their characteristics on the right [SFTP, TFTP, DNS, DHCP, ICMP] •Enables the use of SSH keys to prevent impostor from connecting to the server. •Ensures data integrity and data security for the file transfers using port 22. •Enables backup of network and router configuration files using UDP. •Transfer small files within a LAN using port 69. •Perform a query to translate companypro.net to an IP Address. •Assign the reserved IP Address 10.10.10.200 to a web server at your company. •Perform a ping to ensure that a server is responding to network connections. Match each item to its correct description.
answers: SFTP → SSH key file transfer, port 22
DNS → Resolves domain names to IP addresses
DHCP → Reserves a server IP address

pairs.target: Resolves domain names to IP addresses

questions.explanation:
Match each description to its protocol:

• "SSH keys prevent impostors" + "data integrity and security on port 22" → SFTP. It runs over SSH, so it uses SSH keys and port 22 and encrypts everything.
• "Backup network/router configuration files using UDP" + "transfer small files within a LAN using port 69" → TFTP. Trivial File Transfer Protocol: very simple, UDP port 69, no login and no encryption, so it is only used inside a trusted LAN (for example to back up a router config or load an IOS image).
• "Translate companypro.net to an IP address" → DNS (port 53). The internet's phonebook: name → IP.
• "Assign the reserved IP 10.10.10.200 to a web server" → DHCP. A DHCP RESERVATION ties one IP address to a device's MAC address, so that device (like a web server) always receives the same address.
• "Perform a ping to ensure a server is responding" → ICMP. Ping sends ICMP Echo Request and the server answers with Echo Reply.

💡 Memory: S = Secure (22) · T = Tiny (69) · D-N-S = Domain Name System (names) · D-H-C-P = hands out addresses · I-C-M-P = ping/errors.
💡 Also true: tracert/traceroute rely on ICMP messages, too.

questions.question: Move each protocol or device type from the list on the left to the correct OSI layer on the right. Protocol and Device Type. • Physical SMTP, FTP • Data Link TCP,UDP • Network Cable Hub, NIC • Application Switch • Transport Router Match each item to its correct description.
questions.explanation:
Match each item to the OSI layer where it works:

• SMTP, FTP → Application (L7). These are programs/services that users and apps talk to (email sending, file transfer).
• TCP, UDP → Transport (L4). They carry the port numbers and decide reliable (TCP) vs fast (UDP).
• Cable, hub, NIC → Physical (L1). They only deal with electrical/light signals and bits. A hub just repeats bits to every port. (A NIC really touches L1 and L2, but exam questions file it under Physical.)
• Switch → Data Link (L2). It reads MAC addresses and builds the MAC table.
• Router → Network (L3). It reads IP addresses and chooses the best path between networks.

💡 Easy rule: devices = Hub (1), Switch (2), Router (3). Protocols: ports = 4, IP = 3, MAC = 2.
💡 A Layer 3 (multilayer) switch can do both L2 switching and L3 routing.

questions.question: Move each protocol from the list on the left to the correct TCP/IP model layer on the right. • TCP Internetwork • IP Application • FTP Transport • Network Ethernet Match each item to its correct description.
questions.explanation:
TCP/IP has only 4 layers. Match:

• FTP → Application layer (it is a user-facing service; the TCP/IP Application layer combines OSI layers 5, 6 and 7).
• TCP → Transport layer (ports, reliability).
• IP → Internet layer (some books say "Internetwork"). This is IP addressing and routing = OSI Layer 3.
• Ethernet → Network Access layer (also called Link). It covers cables + frames = OSI Layers 1 and 2.

💡 Mapping: TCP/IP Application = OSI 5-6-7 · Transport = 4 · Internet = 3 · Network Access = 2 + 1.

questions.question: Move each category on the left to its correct definition on the right LAN PAN WAN •Connects devices such as computers, telephones, tables, and printers within a range of about 10 meters. •Spans a small area such as a room, home, office building or small group of building. •Spans a large geographical distance and connects smaller networks over leased lines and VPN’s or tunnels. Match each item to its correct description.
answers: PAN → Personal devices within about 10 meters
questions.explanation:
Match by SIZE of the network:

• About 10 meters, connects personal devices (computers, phones, tablets, printers) → PAN (Personal Area Network). Example: Bluetooth between your phone and earbuds.
• A small area: room, home, office building or a small group of buildings → LAN (Local Area Network). Usually owned and run by one person or company.
• Very large geographic distance, connects smaller networks using leased lines, VPNs or tunnels → WAN (Wide Area Network). The internet is the biggest WAN.

💡 Order small → big: PAN → LAN → (CAN campus) → (MAN city) → WAN. WAN links usually belong to a service provider and you rent them.

1) Start with the question: Decide whether the device is a client, server or relay. A new IPv4 client initially lacks a usable address and may not know a DHCP server. The server leases an address with configuration such as the mask, gateway and DNS servers.
2) Work through it: Follow DORA: Discover locates servers, Offer proposes a lease, Request identifies the chosen offer, and Acknowledgment confirms it. Initial discovery and selection use broadcast behavior; a renewal toward a known server can use unicast.
3) Apply the distinction: Check the layer named in the question. The IPv4 limited broadcast is 255.255.255.255; the Ethernet broadcast is FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. DHCP uses UDP server port 67 and client port 68. A relay forwards client requests between subnets because routers do not normally forward local broadcasts.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not confuse an offer with final confirmation, or renewal with rebinding/expiration. A 169.254.x.x self-assigned address usually indicates that no usable DHCP lease was obtained. On Cisco IOS, show ip dhcp binding displays server leases; ip address dhcp makes an interface a client.

questions.question: Which command will display all the current operational settings configured on a Cisco router?
questions.explanation:
✅ show running-config displays the CURRENT, active configuration of the router (the one stored in RAM and being used right now). That is the "current operational settings".

❌ show startup-config → shows the SAVED configuration in NVRAM, the one loaded at the next boot. It can differ from what's running if you didn't save.
❌ show version → shows IOS version, uptime, hardware model, memory and the configuration register, not the settings.
❌ show protocols → only a short summary of Layer 3 protocol status per interface.

💡 Save your work with: copy running-config startup-config. If you forget and the router reboots, the changes disappear.

1) Start with the question: Determine whether the question asks for local addressing, routing, name resolution or interface state. Commands reveal different evidence, so a valid command can still be the wrong tool for the requested fact.
2) Work through it: On Windows, ipconfig /all reports local IP configuration and DNS servers; route print reports routing entries; nslookup queries DNS; tracert probes the sequence of responding routers. Ping checks reachability using ICMP, not every application service.
3) Apply the distinction: On Cisco IOS, show ip interface brief provides a compact overview of interface addressing and status. A DHCP binding display lists leases known to that DHCP server. Read the device/operating-system context before choosing syntax.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not assume a successful ping proves DNS works or an application is reachable. A missing traceroute response may mean filtering, not a failed router. Configuration output and operational state answer different questions.

questions.question: For each statement, choose True or False.
statements: High levels of network latency decrease network bandwidth.
Low bandwidth can increase network latency.
You can increase throughput by decreasing network latency.
statementNotes: Latency is delay; it does not change a link’s rated bandwidth capacity. It can affect achieved throughput, especially during round trips.
A low-capacity link can add transmission and queuing delay under load. Bandwidth and latency are different measures, but limited capacity can contribute to longer delays.
Reducing latency can improve achieved throughput, especially for traffic that needs acknowledgements. Throughput also depends on bandwidth, loss, congestion, and endpoints.
questions.explanation:
1. False — Latency is delay; it does not change a link’s rated bandwidth capacity. It can affect achieved throughput, especially during round trips.
2. True — A low-capacity link can add transmission and queuing delay under load. Bandwidth and latency are different measures, but limited capacity can contribute to longer delays.
3. True — Reducing latency can improve achieved throughput, especially for traffic that needs acknowledgements. Throughput also depends on bandwidth, loss, congestion, and endpoints.

1) Start with the question: Grade each statement independently against the exhibit. One false statement does not change the truth of another.
2) Statement 1: Latency is delay; it does not change a link’s rated bandwidth capacity. It can affect achieved throughput, especially during round trips.
3) Statement 2: A low-capacity link can add transmission and queuing delay under load. Bandwidth and latency are different measures, but limited capacity can contribute to longer delays.
4) Statement 3: Reducing latency can improve achieved throughput, especially for traffic that needs acknowledgements. Throughput also depends on bandwidth, loss, congestion, and endpoints.
❌ Common mix-ups: Operational status, administrative configuration and address-assignment method are different columns. Read the exact interface named in each statement. All three responses must be correct for the grouped card.

questions.question: Move each cloud computing service model from the list on the left to the correct example on the right. LAAS SAAS PAAS •A company develops application using cloud-based resources and tools. •These virtual machines are connected by a virtual network in the cloud •User access a web-based graphics design application in the cloud for a monthly fee Match each item to its correct description.
questions.explanation:
Match the cloud SERVICE MODEL to what you get:

• IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) → you rent the "raw" building blocks: virtual machines, virtual network and storage, pay as you go. You install and manage the OS and software yourself. Example: Amazon EC2, Azure VMs.
• PaaS (Platform as a Service) → the provider gives the hardware PLUS the tools/runtime/databases so developers can build, run and manage their own applications without managing servers. Example: Azure App Service, Google App Engine.
• SaaS (Software as a Service) → a finished application delivered over the internet, usually for a monthly fee. You just log in and use it. Example: Gmail, Office 365, Canva, a web-based graphics design app.

So: "a company develops an app using cloud tools" = PaaS · "virtual machines connected by a virtual network" = IaaS · "web-based graphics design app for a monthly fee" = SaaS.

💡 Pizza trick: IaaS = rent the kitchen · PaaS = kitchen + tools, you cook · SaaS = order the finished pizza. The further down the list, the less you manage.

questions.question: Which protocol does an IPv6 host use to resolve the MAC address associated with a destination IPv6 address?
questions.explanation:
✅ IPv6 has no ARP. A host uses NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol): it sends a Neighbor Solicitation (an ICMPv6 message) asking "who has this IPv6 address?" and the owner replies with a Neighbor Advertisement containing its MAC address.

❌ ARP → does the same job, but ONLY for IPv4.
❌ CDP → Cisco Discovery Protocol: discovers directly connected Cisco devices; it doesn't map IPs to MACs.
❌ DHCP → gives out IP configuration, doesn't resolve MAC addresses.

💡 Memory: ARP = IPv4 · NDP = IPv6. Both answer "I know the IP, what is the MAC?".

3) Apply the distinction: Link-local addresses come from FE80::/10 and operate on a local link. IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement to resolve link-layer information; IPv4 uses ARP instead.

questions.question: Which protocol is used by IPV6 enabled host to perform automatic stateless address configuration?
questions.explanation:
✅ SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) is how an IPv6 host builds its own address, and it works using ICMPv6 messages:
1) The host sends a Router Solicitation (RS): "any routers here?"
2) The router replies with a Router Advertisement (RA) that carries the network prefix (and default gateway info).
3) The host adds its own interface ID to that prefix and creates its address. No server keeps a list of who has what, hence "stateless".

❌ DHCPv6 → this is the STATEFUL method: a server hands out and tracks addresses.
❌ TFTP → plain file transfer, nothing to do with addressing.
❌ DNS → turns names into addresses, doesn't configure addresses.

💡 Stateless = ICMPv6 (SLAAC). Stateful = DHCPv6. SLAAC uses ICMPv6 Router Solicitation/Advertisement messages. DHCPv6 is a separate, stateful address-configuration option; TFTP transfers files.

questions.question: A user initiates a trouble ticket stating that an external web page is not loading. You determine that other resources both internal and external are still reachable. Which command can you use to help locate where the issue is in the network path to the external web page?
questions.explanation:
✅ tracert (Linux/Mac: traceroute) shows EVERY router (hop) between you and the destination, with the response time of each. You then see where the replies stop. That is exactly "locate where the issue is in the path". How it works: it sends packets with TTL = 1, 2, 3… and each router that drops the packet replies "time exceeded", revealing itself.

❌ ping -t → keeps pinging forever, but only tells you up/down. It doesn't say WHERE the break is.
❌ ipconfig /all → shows YOUR PC's settings (IP, DNS, gateway, MAC). The problem is outside your PC (other sites still work).
❌ nslookup → tests DNS name resolution only. Since other external sites load, DNS is probably fine.

💡 Plan: ping = "are you there?" · tracert = "where does it stop?" · nslookup = "what's the IP of this name?" · ipconfig = "who am I?".

questions.question: Which two statements are true about the IPv4 address of the default gateway configured on a host? (Choose 2.)Note: You will receive partial credit for each correct selection.
options: The IPv4 address of the default gateway must be the first host address in the subnet.
The same default gateway IPv4 address is configured on each host on the local network.
The default gateway is the Loopback0 interface IPv4 address of the router connected to the same local network as the host.
The default gateway is the IPv4 address of the router interface connected to the same local network as the host.
Hosts learn the default gateway IPv4 address through router advertisement messages.
answers: The same default gateway IPv4 address is configured on each host on the local network.
The default gateway is the IPv4 address of the router interface connected to the same local network as the host.
questions.explanation:
✅ Correct pair: "The same default gateway address is configured on each host of the local network" and "The default gateway is the IPv4 address of the router interface connected to the same local network as the host".
• The default gateway is your "door to other networks". Every host on the same LAN uses the SAME door, and that door is the router interface (or Layer 3 switch interface) that sits on THAT LAN.

❌ "Must be the first host address in the subnet" → common habit (.1) but not a rule. Any valid, unused host address of the subnet can be used.
❌ "Is the Loopback0 interface address of the router" → a loopback is a virtual interface inside the router. Hosts cannot reach it as a door. The gateway must be the connected (LAN-side) interface.
❌ "Hosts learn the gateway through router advertisement messages" → RA messages belong to IPv6. IPv4 hosts get the gateway from DHCP or from manual configuration.

💡 Without a default gateway a host can only talk to devices in its own subnet.

questions.question: An engineer configured a new VLAN named VLAN2 for the Data Center team. When the team tries to ping addresses outside VLAN2 from a computer in VLAN2, they are unable to reach them. What should the engineer configure?
questions.explanation:
✅ Default gateway. A computer decides: "is the destination in my own subnet?" If NO, it sends the packet to its default gateway. VLAN2 is a separate network, so the hosts in VLAN2 need a default gateway (the router interface or the Layer 3 switch VLAN interface/SVI for VLAN2) to reach anything outside.

❌ Additional VLAN → more VLANs add more separation, not more reachability.
❌ Default route → a route 0.0.0.0/0 is configured on ROUTERS ("send unknown traffic here"). The hosts in this question need a gateway setting, which is the host's version of that idea.
❌ Static route → a manually typed route on a router for one specific network. It doesn't solve the missing exit for the hosts.

💡 Rule: different VLAN = different subnet = needs a router/Layer 3 device + a default gateway on the hosts to communicate.

1) Start with the question: Start with the host’s view: it needs a stable default gateway even when one router fails. A first-hop redundancy group supplies a virtual gateway, backed by multiple physical routers. The host uses the virtual IP and the associated virtual MAC.
2) Work through it: For HSRP, identify the active router that forwards and the elected standby that is ready to replace it. Higher priority is preferred; preemption allows an eligible higher-priority router to reclaim the active role. Default hello/hold timers are three and ten seconds unless configured otherwise.
3) Apply the distinction: Trace failure in order: the active device fails, the standby misses hellos, the standby becomes active, then forwarding continues using the virtual identity. The host should not need a different gateway address because a physical router changed.
❌ Common mix-ups: Keep protocol families distinct: HSRP is Cisco proprietary, VRRP is standards-based, and GLBP combines redundancy with gateway load sharing. Priority influences election, while the operational state shows what a router is doing now. A higher priority alone does not prove it is currently active.

questions.question: Which information is included in the header of a UDP segment?
questions.explanation:
✅ A UDP header is very small (only 8 bytes) and has just 4 fields: source PORT number, destination PORT number, length, and checksum. So "port numbers" is the answer.

❌ IP addresses → live in the IP header (Layer 3), not in the UDP segment.
❌ MAC addresses → live in the Ethernet frame header (Layer 2).
❌ Sequence numbers → belong to TCP (they are used to put data in order and resend lost data). UDP does none of that; it is "connectionless": just send and hope.

💡 Why does UDP exist? Because it is fast and light. It is used for DNS queries, DHCP, VoIP calls, video streaming and online games, where speed matters more than perfect delivery.

questions.question: What is the purpose of assigning an IP address to the management VLAN interface on a Layer 2 switch?
options: To enable access to the CLI on the switch through Telnet or SSH
To enable the switch to provide DHCP services to other switches in the network
To enable the switch to act as a default gateway for the attached devices
To enable the switch to resolve URLs for the attached the devices
answers: To enable access to the CLI on the switch through Telnet or SSH
questions.explanation:
✅ A Layer 2 switch has no IP address on its normal ports. Giving the management VLAN interface (SVI) an IP address lets YOU reach the switch over the network to manage it, using SSH (recommended, encrypted) or Telnet (plain text), instead of walking to the console cable.

❌ Act as a default gateway for attached devices → a Layer 2 switch doesn't route; the management IP does not turn it into a gateway.
❌ Provide DHCP services to other switches → not a feature of a basic L2 switch.
❌ Resolve URLs/DNS for attached devices → a DNS server does that.

💡 The management IP is like the switch's "phone number" for the administrator. The switch also needs a default gateway configured if you want to manage it from another network.

1) Start with the question: Identify the asset and the type of harm. A data breach exposes confidential information; denial of service attacks availability. A VPN secures a connection across an untrusted network; a firewall inspects or controls traffic; NAC controls network admission.
2) Work through it: Match the control to the threat. SSH protects a management session from plaintext exposure. BPDU guard detects unexpected spanning-tree messages on an edge port. DHCP snooping applies trust and rate limits to DHCP traffic, while DAI checks ARP information using relevant bindings and validation rules.
3) Apply the distinction: For a configuration question, ask what a packet or frame will actually experience: blocked admission, encrypted transport, inspection, rate limiting, or an interface shutdown. Products may combine functions, but that does not make all terms interchangeable.
❌ Common mix-ups: A classroom statement about a product’s main role is not a claim that no model can integrate another feature. Keep any source-key caution: a technically questionable answer should not be justified just because the saved review selected it.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)?
options: prevents loops in a network by blocking redundant links.
provides load balancing across multiple paths in a network.
prioritizes network traffic based on Quality of Service (QoS) settings.
allows for rapid convergence by eliminating the need for spanning tree calculations.
answers: prevents loops in a network by blocking redundant links.
questions.explanation:
✅ STP (Spanning Tree Protocol, IEEE 802.1D) prevents Layer 2 loops. When switches are connected with redundant links, a broadcast could circle forever (a "broadcast storm") and crash the network. STP chooses a root bridge and puts redundant ports into a BLOCKING state, keeping a loop-free tree. If an active link fails, a blocked one wakes up as a backup.

❌ Load balancing across paths → STP does the opposite: it blocks extra paths (it keeps them as backups).
❌ Prioritizing traffic by QoS → that is QoS, a different feature.
❌ Rapid convergence by eliminating spanning-tree calculations → RSTP converges faster, but STP never removes its calculations.

💡 Remember: STP = "stop the loops" (amber port LED often = blocked by STP).

1) Start with the question: Separate election, port role and port state. STP removes Layer 2 forwarding loops while preserving physical redundancy. Ethernet frames have no hop limit that would safely stop a broadcast circulating around a switching loop.
2) Work through it: For root election, compare the complete bridge IDs: lower bridge priority wins, with the MAC address breaking a remaining tie. On a non-root switch, compare root-path costs to find the root port. The designated port is the best forwarding path for a particular segment.
3) Apply the distinction: Match the version to the clue: legacy STP uses a shared tree, PVST+ builds per-VLAN trees, Rapid PVST+ applies faster RSTP behavior per VLAN, and MST maps VLAN groups into instances. In classic STP, learning builds the MAC table without forwarding user frames; forwarding does both.
❌ Common mix-ups: Bridge ID and path cost are different quantities. PortFast speeds an endpoint port’s transition; it does not switch off STP or make a switch-to-switch loop safe. When reading an exhibit, use its actual priority, MAC and cost values rather than the switch name.

questions.question: What packets does OSPF use to discover neighbors and form adjacencies?
options: Hello packets carried directly over IP
answers: Hello packets carried directly over IP
questions.explanation:
OSPF neighbors discover one another with Hello packets. OSPF is carried directly over IP protocol 89; the source answer choices had a broken label, so they were repaired.

1) Start with the question: Identify the protocol that builds the route and the packet that establishes its neighbor relationship. OSPF is a link-state routing protocol; it exchanges information about topology to calculate routes.
2) Work through it: OSPF Hello packets discover and maintain neighbors. Peers must agree on relevant settings before they can establish the required relationship. A Hello is a routing-protocol message carried over IP, not an ordinary TCP application handshake.
3) Apply the distinction: Separate neighbor discovery from data forwarding. A router subsequently uses the routing table to forward packets according to destination prefixes. The existence of a Hello packet does not alone prove every route or full adjacency is established.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not confuse OSPF Hellos with DHCP discovery or ICMP echo requests. Those messages configure hosts or probe reachability; they do not perform the same neighbor-management job.

questions.question: What information is contained in the MAC address table of a switch?
options: Dynamically learned Layer2 and Layer3 addresses of devices communicating on active ports on the switch
The MAC addresses of devices communicating on active ports and static MAC addresses configured by the administrator
All active ports on the switch and the host Layer3 addresses that were dynamically learned on each port.
MAC addresses to IP Address mappings learned through ARP requests or manually configured by the administrator
answers: The MAC addresses of devices communicating on active ports and static MAC addresses configured by the administrator
questions.explanation:
✅ A switch's MAC address table lists MAC address ↔ switch port (and VLAN). Entries are learned dynamically when a frame arrives (the switch reads the SOURCE MAC and notes the port), but an administrator can also add static entries. So option B (the dynamic + static MAC addresses on active ports) is correct.

❌ "Layer 2 AND Layer 3 addresses" → a switch only learns Layer 2 (MAC) addresses, not IP addresses.
❌ "All active ports and the host Layer 3 addresses…" → again, IP addresses are not stored here.
❌ "MAC-to-IP mappings learned through ARP" → that is the ARP table on a PC or router, not the switch's MAC table.

💡 How the switch uses it: known destination → send only to that port · unknown destination or broadcast → flood to all ports except the one it arrived on. The entries expire after a while (aging, default 300 seconds).

questions.question: What is the purpose of a subnet mask?
options: determine the network portion of an IP address
determine the host portion of an IP address
determine the default gateway for a network
determine the DNS server for a network
answers: determine the network portion of an IP address
questions.explanation:
✅ The subnet mask tells a device which part of an IP address is the NETWORK portion (the 1-bits) and which part is the HOST portion (the 0-bits). With that, a PC can decide whether another IP is on its own network (talk directly) or on another network (send to the default gateway).

Example: 192.168.1.10 with 255.255.255.0 → network 192.168.1.0, host .10.

❌ Default gateway → configured separately (it is the router's IP).
❌ DNS server → also configured separately (turns names into IPs).
❌ "Determine the host portion" is only half-true: the mask does separate the host bits too, but the expected exam answer is that it determines the NETWORK portion.

1) Start with the question: Start with the prefix or subnet mask, not the host’s last octet. Each 255 mask octet contributes eight network bits; partial octets contribute the number of leading binary ones. For example, 252 is 11111100, which contributes six network bits.
2) Work through it: Compute the address count from host bits: 2^(32 − prefix) total IPv4 addresses. In an ordinary multi-access subnet, subtract the network and broadcast addresses to get usable hosts. Then subtract explicitly excluded/reserved addresses that actually fall inside that subnet, counting each only once.
3) Apply the distinction: Treat exclusion ranges as inclusive: last − first + 1. A /24 normally has 254 usable addresses, /25 has 126, /26 has 62, and /27 has 30. An excluded gateway address is a reservation, not an additional network/broadcast deduction.
❌ Common mix-ups: A reservation and an active lease are not the same thing. Check whether the requested answer is total addresses, usable hosts or remaining leases. For /31 and /32, ordinary network/broadcast subtraction is not applied in the same way; use the context stated in the question.

questions.question: A user at you company cannot connect to website on the internet. However, they can connect to network resources on the company LAN. You want to use the divide and conquer approach to troubleshoot the issue. What should you do first?
options: Run the Telnet command from the user’s computer
Ping the default gateway from the user’s computer
answers: Ping the default gateway from the user’s computer
questions.explanation:
✅ Ping the default gateway first. The user can reach LAN resources, so cables, NIC and local switching are OK (Layers 1–2). The problem is "somewhere towards the internet". Divide and conquer starts in the middle: the gateway is the middle point of the path.
• Ping gateway works → the local side is fine; the issue is beyond the router (ISP, DNS, route, firewall) → go further out.
• Ping gateway fails → the issue is local (gateway config, IP/mask/gateway settings) → go back toward the PC.

❌ Check cable connections / network adapter → those are bottom-up steps (Layer 1) and the LAN already works, so they are very unlikely.
❌ Telnet → a remote management tool, not the right first test.

💡 Top-down = start at applications · Bottom-up = start at cables · Divide and conquer = start in the middle and move up or down according to the result.

1) Start with the question: Start with the host’s view: it needs a stable default gateway even when one router fails. A first-hop redundancy group supplies a virtual gateway, backed by multiple physical routers. The host uses the virtual IP and the associated virtual MAC.
2) Work through it: For HSRP, identify the active router that forwards and the elected standby that is ready to replace it. Higher priority is preferred; preemption allows an eligible higher-priority router to reclaim the active role. Default hello/hold timers are three and ten seconds unless configured otherwise.
3) Apply the distinction: Trace failure in order: the active device fails, the standby misses hellos, the standby becomes active, then forwarding continues using the virtual identity. The host should not need a different gateway address because a physical router changed.
❌ Common mix-ups: Keep protocol families distinct: HSRP is Cisco proprietary, VRRP is standards-based, and GLBP combines redundancy with gateway load sharing. Priority influences election, while the operational state shows what a router is doing now. A higher priority alone does not prove it is currently active.

questions.question: Your company has 20 Cisco switches throughout its building. You need to view the configuration of each switch from the command line. Which protocol should you use?
questions.explanation:
✅ Of the four choices, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the network-management protocol, used to monitor and manage many devices from a central system (NMS).

❌ FTP → transfers files. ❌ RDP → remote desktop of Windows computers. ❌ SMTP → sends email.

💡 This is a weak question. For "view the configuration from the command line", SSH (or Telnet) would be the more natural answer if offered. Real-world: SSH to each switch for the CLI; SNMP for monitoring/statistics.

1) Start with the question: Determine whether the question asks for local addressing, routing, name resolution or interface state. Commands reveal different evidence, so a valid command can still be the wrong tool for the requested fact.
2) Work through it: On Windows, ipconfig /all reports local IP configuration and DNS servers; route print reports routing entries; nslookup queries DNS; tracert probes the sequence of responding routers. Ping checks reachability using ICMP, not every application service.
3) Apply the distinction: On Cisco IOS, show ip interface brief provides a compact overview of interface addressing and status. A DHCP binding display lists leases known to that DHCP server. Read the device/operating-system context before choosing syntax.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not assume a successful ping proves DNS works or an application is reachable. A missing traceroute response may mean filtering, not a failed router. Configuration output and operational state answer different questions.

questions.question: Which device protects the network by permitting or denying traffic based on IP address, port number, or application?
questions.explanation:
✅ A firewall permits or denies traffic using rules based on IP address, port number, protocol (and for next-generation firewalls, even the application).

❌ Access point → a device that gives wireless devices access to the wired network. It doesn't filter traffic by rule.
❌ VPN gateway → ends encrypted tunnels (remote users or sites). It protects the privacy of traffic, but it is not the rule-based filter.
❌ Intrusion Detection System (IDS) → only watches and alerts; it doesn't block. (An IPS does block.)

💡 Firewall = the security guard at the door with a list of who can go through.

questions.question: How does a firewall determine which traffic to block?
options: The firewall matches traffic based on the IP address in the ARP table
The firewall performs a one-to-many network address translation
The firewall matches the traffic based on source and destination IP address
The firewall performs a one-to-one network address translation.
answers: The firewall matches the traffic based on source and destination IP address
questions.explanation:
✅ A firewall matches each packet against its rules: source IP, destination IP, port, and protocol (permit or deny). Many firewalls end with an implicit "deny everything else".

❌ ARP table → used by devices to find MAC addresses; a firewall doesn't decide using it.
❌ One-to-many NAT (PAT/overload) and one-to-one NAT → NAT translates addresses (hides private IPs behind public ones). It is not how a firewall chooses what to block.

💡 Typical rule: "Permit TCP from any to 10.0.0.5 port 443; deny all others".

questions.question: Which action can a network firewall directly perform using a traffic rule?
options: Block traffic to a specified port
Prevent a user from launching an app on their PC
answers: Block traffic to a specified port
questions.explanation:
Three statements about a network firewall:

1) "Can block traffic to specific ports on internal computers" → TRUE. Rules can deny, for example, port 23 (Telnet) or 3389 (RDP).
2) "Can direct all web traffic to a specific IP address" → TRUE. This is port forwarding / NAT: traffic arriving on port 80/443 is sent to a chosen internal server.
3) "Can prevent specific apps from running on a computer" → FALSE. A NETWORK firewall only filters traffic passing through it. It cannot see or stop programs running locally on a PC. That is the job of antivirus / endpoint security / application control.

💡 Network firewall = controls traffic between networks. Endpoint security = controls what runs on the device. A firewall can block traffic by port and can forward traffic when a destination-NAT or port-forwarding rule is configured. Blocking an application from running is an endpoint-control function.

questions.question: Which best describes confidentiality with regards to network security?
options: Ensures data is available for access by providing redundant systems.
Ensures data is not changed during transit between system.
Ensures data is kept secret using safeguards to prevent unauthorized access.
Ensures data is trusted and has not been tampered with or changed
answers: Ensures data is kept secret using safeguards to prevent unauthorized access.
questions.explanation:
✅ Confidentiality = keeping data SECRET so only authorized people can read it (encryption, access control, strong authentication).

❌ "Providing redundant systems so data is available" → AVAILABILITY.
❌ "Data is not changed during transit" → INTEGRITY.
❌ "Data is trusted and has not been tampered with" → INTEGRITY.

💡 CIA triad: C = Confidential (secret) · I = Integrity (unchanged) · A = Availability (up when needed). Keyword "secret/private/unauthorized access" → Confidentiality.

questions.question: Which component of the AAA service security model provides identify verification?
questions.explanation:
✅ Authentication = verifying WHO you are (username/password, MFA, certificate, biometrics).

❌ Authorization → decides WHAT you are allowed to do after you are identified (permissions).
❌ Accounting → records WHAT you did (logs of logins, commands, time used).
❌ Auditing → not a part of AAA. It is a general review process (and the "A" for tracking is called Accounting).

💡 Building analogy: Authentication = showing your ID at the door · Authorization = which rooms your badge opens · Accounting = the visitor logbook.

1) Start with the question: Determine whether the question asks about identity, permission or an activity record. Authentication checks who the user is; authorization decides which requested actions are allowed; accounting records use and activity. They solve different parts of access control.
2) Work through it: Map the wording: usernames/passwords point to authentication, allowed commands/resources point to authorization, and logs or usage reports point to accounting. Local AAA keeps credential information on the device; server-based AAA centralizes it through a service such as RADIUS or TACACS+.
3) Apply the distinction: For 802.1X, name the three roles: the supplicant requests access, the switch or AP acts as authenticator, and the authentication server validates the request. Enterprise Wi-Fi commonly uses this arrangement so each user has an individual identity.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not treat SSH, HTTPS, RADIUS and SNMP as interchangeable. SSH/HTTPS protect management sessions, RADIUS supports AAA exchanges, and SNMP is used for monitoring/management. A source key that assigns the wrong job to one of these protocols needs a warning, not an invented justification.

questions.question: When setting up a wireless network which security benefit is provided by enabling WPA3?
options: Limits network access to only specified devices
Sends traffic through an encrypted tunnel
Secures authentication between client and access point
Makes it more difficult to discover wireless network
answers: Secures authentication between client and access point
questions.explanation:
✅ WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) as a new handshake between the client and the access point. It protects the password-based login even if someone records the traffic and tries to guess the password offline, and it gives each session its own keys. That is "secures authentication between client and access point".

❌ "Limits access to specified devices" → that is MAC filtering.
❌ "Sends traffic through an encrypted tunnel" → that describes a VPN.
❌ "Makes it more difficult to discover the network" → that is hiding the SSID.

💡 Wi-Fi security order (old → new): WEP → WPA → WPA2 (AES) → WPA3 (SAE). Higher = better.

1) Start with the question: Identify whether the question concerns an AP, a controller, or discovery by a client. An AP provides wireless access to the LAN. A WLC centrally manages controller-based APs; an autonomous AP is configured independently.
2) Work through it: For controller-based operation, distinguish control/management from client traffic. CAPWAP provides AP-to-controller communication and can encapsulate client traffic. LWAPP is older terminology found in the course material. Controller screens and available interface options depend on the software version.
3) Apply the distinction: For discovery, a beacon advertises a WLAN, while a client probe request actively searches. A non-advertised SSID may require a client to name it explicitly. An SSID identifies a network; the administrator password protects management and the wireless credentials protect admission.
❌ Common mix-ups: Hiding an SSID is not encryption or strong access control. Bluetooth support is model-dependent rather than the definition of an AP. A controller is not just a replacement name for an AP, and choosing the correct SSID is different from validating credentials.

questions.question: Move the CIA security principles from the list on the left to its example on the right. Confidentiality- Integrity- Availability You generate a digital signature and attach it to a message You encrypt a sensitive email message You configure three redundant web servers at your company - Match each item to its correct description.
questions.explanation:
Match each action to the CIA principle:

• "Generate a digital signature and attach it to a message" → INTEGRITY. A signature (and a hash) proves the message wasn't changed and shows who sent it.
• "Encrypt a sensitive email message" → CONFIDENTIALITY. Only the person with the key can read it.
• "Configure three redundant web servers" → AVAILABILITY. If one server dies, the others keep the site up.

💡 Think "what is the goal?": secret = C · unchanged = I · always up = A.

questions.question: Move the MFA factors from the list on the left to their correct examples on he right Factors: Possession , Inference, Knowledge Specifying your name and password to log on to a service Entering a one-time security code send to your device after logging in Holding your phone to your face to be recognized Match each item to its correct description.
questions.explanation:
Match each example to the MFA factor (the kind of proof):

• Name and password → KNOWLEDGE (something you know).
• One-time code sent to your device → POSSESSION (something you have: phone, token).
• Phone recognizes your face → INHERENCE (something you are: face, fingerprint, iris).

The slide's option list says "Inference": that's a typo. The factor is called Inherence.

💡 MFA means two or MORE DIFFERENT factors. Password + PIN = still only "knowledge" twice, so it is NOT MFA. Password + phone code = MFA. The source says “Inference”; the correct name is inherence, a biometric factor (“something you are”).

1) Start with the question: Separate proof of identity from permission. A password is one knowledge factor; a second independent factor makes a stolen password alone less useful. Authentication is followed by authorization of resources and actions.
2) Work through it: Multifactor authentication combines distinct factors, such as something you know and something you have. Two different passwords are still the same kind of factor, so they do not provide the same separation.
3) Apply the distinction: Consider the threat in the question: if a password is exposed, a required second factor can prevent immediate account use. Prefer phishing-resistant methods when available; recovery methods must also be protected.
❌ Common mix-ups: MFA does not replace patching, access restrictions or activity auditing. It reduces particular account-takeover risks, while authorization and accounting address what an authenticated account may do and what it actually did.

questions.question: Move the security options from the list on the left to its characteristics on the right. You may use each security option once, more than once, or not at all. Security Options: WEP, WPA2- Personal, WPA-Enterprise Uses a minimum of 40 bits for encryption Use a RADIU Server for authentication Use AES and a pre-shared key for authentication Match each item to its correct description.
questions.explanation:
Match the Wi-Fi security option to its characteristic:

• "Uses a minimum of 40 bits for encryption" → WEP. The oldest option (40-bit or 104-bit RC4 keys). It is broken and obsolete.
• "Uses a RADIUS server for authentication" → WPA-Enterprise. Each user logs in with their own credentials through 802.1X and a RADIUS server (companies, schools).
• "Uses AES and a pre-shared key" → WPA2-Personal. Everyone shares the same Wi-Fi password (PSK) and encryption uses AES (homes, small offices).

💡 Personal = one shared password (PSK) · Enterprise = RADIUS + individual logins · WEP = never use.

questions.question: You need to configure wireless settings for a home router. Move the actions from the list on the left to the correct scenarios on the right. • You want to prevent users from using the pushbutton method for accessing the. • You want devices to use a pre-shared key when connecting to the network. • You want to prevent devices from discovering the name of the WIFI network o Set the security mode to WPA2-PSK o Disable SSID broadcasting o Disable WPS Match each item to its correct description.
answers: Set WPA2-PSK → Use a pre-shared key
Disable SSID broadcast → Hide Wi-Fi name
questions.explanation:
Match the goal to the setting:

• Stop users from connecting with the push-button method → DISABLE WPS. WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) lets you join by pressing a button or typing a short PIN; the PIN is easy to brute-force, so turn it off.
• Devices use a pre-shared key when connecting → SET SECURITY MODE TO WPA2-PSK. PSK = pre-shared key = the Wi-Fi password.
• Stop devices from discovering the name of the Wi-Fi network → DISABLE SSID BROADCASTING. The access point no longer announces its name (this only hides the name; it's weak security by itself).

💡 The tiny labels on the slide for scenarios 1 and 3 are swapped (your "Baligtad" note is right). Use the pairing above. The notebook notes the first and third labels are swapped. The corrected actions are disable WPS for push-button access and disable SSID broadcasting to hide the network name.

1) Start with the question: Identify whether the question concerns an AP, a controller, or discovery by a client. An AP provides wireless access to the LAN. A WLC centrally manages controller-based APs; an autonomous AP is configured independently.
2) Work through it: For controller-based operation, distinguish control/management from client traffic. CAPWAP provides AP-to-controller communication and can encapsulate client traffic. LWAPP is older terminology found in the course material. Controller screens and available interface options depend on the software version.
3) Apply the distinction: For discovery, a beacon advertises a WLAN, while a client probe request actively searches. A non-advertised SSID may require a client to name it explicitly. An SSID identifies a network; the administrator password protects management and the wireless credentials protect admission.
❌ Common mix-ups: Hiding an SSID is not encryption or strong access control. Bluetooth support is model-dependent rather than the definition of an AP. A controller is not just a replacement name for an AP, and choosing the correct SSID is different from validating credentials.

questions.question: Which component of the AAA service security model provides identity verification?
questions.explanation:
✅ Authentication = verifying WHO you are (username/password, MFA, certificate, biometrics).

❌ Authorization → decides WHAT you are allowed to do after you are identified (permissions).
❌ Accounting → records WHAT you did (logs of logins, commands, time used).
❌ Auditing → not a part of AAA. It is a general review process (and the "A" for tracking is called Accounting).

💡 Building analogy: Authentication = showing your ID at the door · Authorization = which rooms your badge opens · Accounting = the visitor logbook.

1) Start with the question: Determine whether the question asks about identity, permission or an activity record. Authentication checks who the user is; authorization decides which requested actions are allowed; accounting records use and activity. They solve different parts of access control.
2) Work through it: Map the wording: usernames/passwords point to authentication, allowed commands/resources point to authorization, and logs or usage reports point to accounting. Local AAA keeps credential information on the device; server-based AAA centralizes it through a service such as RADIUS or TACACS+.
3) Apply the distinction: For 802.1X, name the three roles: the supplicant requests access, the switch or AP acts as authenticator, and the authentication server validates the request. Enterprise Wi-Fi commonly uses this arrangement so each user has an individual identity.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not treat SSH, HTTPS, RADIUS and SNMP as interchangeable. SSH/HTTPS protect management sessions, RADIUS supports AAA exchanges, and SNMP is used for monitoring/management. A source key that assigns the wrong job to one of these protocols needs a warning, not an invented justification.

questions.question: Which wireless security option uses a pre-shared key to authenticate clients?
questions.explanation:
✅ WPA2-Personal (WPA2-PSK) authenticates clients with a pre-shared key: one common Wi-Fi password for everyone.

❌ 802.1X → port-based authentication using individual credentials and a RADIUS server (that's what Enterprise uses), not a shared key.
❌ 802.1Q → VLAN tagging on trunk links, not Wi-Fi security.
❌ WPA2-Enterprise → uses 802.1X + RADIUS, not a pre-shared key.

💡 Personal = PSK. Enterprise = 802.1X.

questions.question: You need to connect a computer's network adapter to a switch using a 1000BASE-T cable. Which connector should you use?
questions.explanation:
✅ 1000BASE-T is Gigabit Ethernet over twisted-pair copper cable (Cat5e or better), and twisted-pair copper ends with the RJ-45 connector (8 pins).

❌ Coax → cable-TV-style cable (F-type / BNC connectors).
❌ RJ-11 → smaller connector for telephone lines.
❌ OS2 LC → OS2 is single-mode FIBER and LC is a fiber connector. Wrong medium.

💡 Decoder for "1000BASE-T": 1000 = 1000 Mbps (1 Gbps) · BASE = baseband signaling · T = twisted pair.

1) Start with the question: Identify the transmission medium first. Copper twisted-pair Ethernet uses electrical signals; fiber uses light. The connector must be appropriate to the cable and equipment, not merely have a similar shape.
2) Work through it: UTP Ethernet commonly terminates in an 8-position modular connector called RJ-45 in this course. Fiber interfaces commonly use connectors such as LC. Match the required physical medium and port rather than choosing an interface by a familiar name.
3) Apply the distinction: For troubleshooting, distinguish a physical-layer problem from addressing. A wrong connector, damaged cable or failed link cannot be fixed by changing DNS. Conversely, a link light alone does not prove that the host has a correct IP, mask or gateway.
❌ Common mix-ups: A connector does not by itself determine every supported rate or reach. Cable category, fiber type, transceiver and interface specifications must agree; the question’s stated medium is the first constraint.

questions.question: Which type of connector should you use to terminate unshielded twisted pair (UTP) cable?
questions.explanation:
✅ UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair) cable is terminated with RJ-45 (Registered Jack 45) connectors. This is the plug on a normal network cable.

❌ ST (Straight Tip) → fiber connector, round, twist-lock.
❌ SC (Subscriber Connector) → fiber connector, square, push-pull.
❌ OS2 LC → single-mode fiber (OS2) with a small LC connector.

💡 Copper = RJ-45 (Ethernet) or RJ-11 (phone). Fiber = LC / SC / ST.

questions.question: You want to store files that will be accessible by every user on your network. Which endpoint device do you need?
questions.explanation:
✅ A server is a computer whose job is to share resources (files, printing, web, email, etc.) with other devices. A file server stores files that every user on the network can access.

❌ Access point → gives Wi-Fi devices a connection to the wired network.
❌ Hub → repeats signals to all ports; stores nothing.
❌ Switch → connects devices and forwards frames; stores nothing for users.

💡 Servers and PCs are END devices. Switches, hubs and access points are INTERMEDIARY devices (they move traffic).

questions.question: What type of interface is the administrator installing in the router?
questions.explanation:
✅ SFP = Small Form-factor Pluggable. It is a small, hot-swappable slot where you plug a transceiver module (fiber or copper). It lets a switch/router use different cable types (e.g., fiber for long distance) just by changing the module.

❌ USB → general-purpose port for flash drives, storage or a console connection.
❌ Serial → older WAN/console-style interface.
❌ PoE → not a separate shape: it's an RJ-45 port that also supplies power to a device over the cable.

💡 If you see a small metal module being slid into a slot on a switch/router, it's an SFP.

questions.question: Which Ethernet port feature can deliver both network data and electrical power to an IP phone over one cable?
questions.explanation:
✅ The slide marks the port with number 6. A PoE (Power over Ethernet) port is an RJ-45 Ethernet port that sends DATA and ELECTRICAL POWER through the same twisted-pair cable. It powers IP phones, wireless access points and cameras, so they need no wall adapter.

❌ Ports that are console, SFP or USB don't supply power to an IP phone.

(The switch picture is missing from the PDF, so the numbering can't be verified. When you see the image on the exam, look for RJ-45 ports labeled PoE.)

💡 PoE standards: 802.3af (about 15 W), 802.3at "PoE+" (about 30 W), 802.3bt (60–100 W). The referenced switch exhibit was missing. This version asks about the PoE-capable port function rather than a numbered port that cannot be identified without that picture.

questions.question: Which standard contains the specifications for Wi-Fi networks?
questions.explanation:
✅ IEEE 802.11 is the family of standards for wireless LANs (Wi-Fi).

❌ GSM → older mobile phone (cellular) standard.
❌ LTE → 4G cellular standard.
❌ IEEE 802.3 → Ethernet (wired).
❌ EIA/TIA 568A → standard for cable wiring/pinout (the color order in an RJ-45 plug).

💡 Quick numbers: 802.11 = Wi-Fi · 802.3 = Ethernet · 802.1Q = VLAN tagging · 802.1X = port/network login.

1) Start with the question: Identify the wireless standard, frequency band and capability asked for before comparing choices. A rate, a frequency and an antenna feature describe different properties, so two statements can both be true while only one is offered in a particular variant.
2) Work through it: Use the core comparison: 802.11b operates at 2.4 GHz up to 11 Mb/s; 802.11g at 2.4 GHz up to 54 Mb/s; 802.11a at 5 GHz up to 54 Mb/s. 802.11n supports 2.4/5 GHz and MIMO, with a maximum theoretical 600 Mb/s; 802.11ac uses 5 GHz.
3) Apply the distinction: Check compatibility before moving clients between bands. A b/g-only client cannot use a 5 GHz radio just because the router is dual-band. Multiple antennas/spatial streams can improve capacity, while interference, shared airtime and protocol overhead reduce real application throughput.
❌ Common mix-ups: Advertised PHY rate is not guaranteed download speed. More channels or less congestion can help a suitable 5 GHz deployment, but it does not make every client compatible. IEEE 802.11 defines the WLAN family; IEEE 802.1Q instead concerns VLAN bridging/tagging.

questions.question: Which device is an Internet of Things (IoT) device?
questions.explanation:
✅ An internet-accessible thermostat is an IoT (Internet of Things) device: a small, "smart" everyday object with sensors/software that connects to the network to send data or be controlled remotely. Other IoT examples: smart doorbells, cameras, light bulbs, wearables.

❌ A video streaming server, a VPN concentrator and a cloud file-storage array are normal network infrastructure/servers, not small IoT devices.

💡 IoT = everyday object + sensor + network connection.

questions.question: Which network technology is not impacted by electromagnetic and radio wave interference?
questions.explanation:
✅ Fiber-optic cable sends LIGHT through glass, so electrical noise (EMI) and radio interference cannot affect it. It also supports very long distances and high speeds.

❌ Wireless → can be disturbed by other signals, microwaves, walls, distance.
❌ Twisted pair and copper → the twists only reduce crosstalk; they are still affected by EMI from motors, fluorescent lights and power cables. (Twisted pair is a type of copper cable, so those two options are really the same family.)

💡 Choose fiber for: long distances, outdoors/underground, factories with heavy electrical noise.

1) Start with the question: Separate coverage from capacity. Coverage asks whether the signal reaches a location reliably; capacity asks how much useful traffic the shared radio channel can carry. A stronger signal does not remove every source of contention or interference.
2) Work through it: Look for the radio clue: microwave ovens can interfere with 2.4 GHz, adjacent/overlapping channels can compete, and walls or distance can weaken a signal. Appropriate channel planning and placing APs closer to users solve different problems.
3) Apply the distinction: An omnidirectional antenna provides coverage around its axis, while a directional antenna concentrates it toward an area. A compatible replaceable antenna can alter a coverage pattern, but client capability, permitted transmit power and the return path still matter.
❌ Common mix-ups: Do not assume that a new antenna creates more internet bandwidth or that 5 GHz always reaches farther. Values such as 1/6/11 refer to a common non-overlapping 20 MHz 2.4 GHz plan; channel width and local regulatory rules also matter.

questions.question: A cisco switch is not accessible from the network. You need to view its running configuration. Which out of band method can you use to access it?
questions.explanation:
✅ The console port is "out-of-band" management: you connect a console cable directly from your laptop to the switch and use a terminal program. It works even when the network is down and the switch has no IP address.

❌ SSH, Telnet and SNMP all go through the network ("in-band"), so they need IP connectivity, which is the very thing that's broken.

💡 Out-of-band = separate path that doesn't rely on the network. Console is the classic example.

questions.question: Examine the connections shown in the following image. Move the cable types on the right to the appropriate connection description on the left. You may use each cable type more than once or not at all. • Straight-through UTP Cable • Fiber Optic • Crossover UTP Cable • Straight-through UTP Match each item to its correct description.
answers: Switch to R1 Gi0/0/1 → Straight-through UTP
R2 to R3 underground conduit → Fiber-optic cable
R1 Gi0/0/0 to R2 Gi0/0/1 → Crossover UTP
Switch S3 to Server0 NIC → Straight-through UTP
questions.explanation:
Pick the cable by the devices on each end:

• Switch → Router R1 (Gi0/0/1) → STRAIGHT-THROUGH. A switch and a router are UNLIKE devices.
• R2 → R3 through an underground conduit → FIBER OPTIC. Long distance, outdoors/underground, and no EMI/lightning problems.
• R1 Gi0/0/0 → R2 Gi0/0/1 → CROSSOVER. Router to router = LIKE devices.
• Switch S3 → Server0 NIC → STRAIGHT-THROUGH. An end device (server) to a switch = unlike devices.

💡 Rule: unlike devices → straight-through (PC–switch, switch–router). Like devices → crossover (switch–switch, router–router, PC–PC). Modern ports auto-sense (Auto-MDIX), but the exam still asks.

questions.question: A local company requires two networks in two new buildings. The addresses used in these networks must be in the private network range. Which two address ranges should the company use? (Choose 2.)
questions.explanation:
✅ Private IPv4 ranges (RFC 1918) are: 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255 (10.0.0.0/8) · 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 (172.16.0.0/12) · 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255 (192.168.0.0/16). So 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 and 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255 are correct.

❌ 192.16.0.0 – 192.16.255.255 → looks similar but it is PUBLIC (the private one is 192.168).
❌ 11.0.0.0 – 11.255.255.255 → PUBLIC (only 10.x is private).

💡 Private addresses are not routed on the internet. To go out, they use NAT, which swaps them for a public address.
